``` ::: ::: For epoxiconazole, the lowest BIC was obtained for the model combining effects on growth and reproduction (BIC = -86.1; @tbl-ResEPX). However, the assimilation-and-reproduction formulation received virtually equivalent support (BIC = -85.9; $\Delta\mathrm{BIC}=0.2$). The assimilation and maintenance model also remained plausible (BIC = -84.2; $\Delta\mathrm{BIC}=1.9$), whereas the assimilation and growth formulation was less supported (BIC = -83.4; $\Delta\mathrm{BIC}=2.7$). The assimilation-only and maintenance-and-growth models received substantially lower support, with $\Delta\mathrm{BIC}$ values above 5. Overall, the available data did not allow a clear statistical distinction between the growth-and-reproduction and assimilation-and-reproduction pMoAs. Because epoxiconazole exposure has been associated with altered energy reserves and impaired reproductive performance [@givaudan_2014; @pelosi_2016; @zarn_2003; @taxvig_2007; @kjaerstad_2010; @echa_2025], the assimilation-and-reproduction formulation was retained as the most biologically plausible representation, while acknowledging the growth-and-reproduction formulation as an equally plausible statistical alternative. The selected assimilation-and-reproduction model estimated a no-effect concentration ($c_0$) of 47,101 \[14,367; 96,352\] ng$\cdot$g$^{-1}$ internal concentration and a stress slope parameter ($b$) of $2.2 \cdot 10^{-6}$ \[$0.9 \cdot 10^{-6}$; $4.7 \cdot 10^{-6}$\] g$\cdot$ng$^{-1}$. The broad credible interval around $c_0$ indicates substantial uncertainty in the internal concentration at which toxic stress begins, whereas the stress slope was comparatively better constrained. ### Chains Chains are plotted for all models. ::: panel-tabset ## A ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Parameters chains. The model captured the general magnitude and shape of the decline in life-history performance with increasing epoxiconazole exposure. However, some systematic deviations remained. Growth effects were underestimated at the lowest tested concentrations, between 0.928 and 9.28 mg$\cdot$kg$^{-1}$, resulting in predicted growth values above the observations. Reproductive effects were also underestimated at the highest concentrations, between 43.1 and 200 mg$\cdot$kg$^{-1}$, with predicted cocoon production exceeding the observed values. concentration-dependent responses observed for juvenile growth, adult growth, and reproduction (@fig-pred_G_EPX_AR_summary_article, @fig-predobs_G_EPX_AR & fig-pred_G_EPX_ARsummary). The model captured the general magnitude and shape of the decline in life-history performance with increasing epoxiconazole exposure. However, some systematic deviations remained. Growth was underestimated at the lowest tested concentrations, between 0.928 and 9.28 mg$\cdot$kg$^{-1}$. Reproductive effects were also underestimated at the highest concentrations, between 43.1 and 200 mg$\cdot$kg$^{-1}$, with predicted cocoon production exceeding the observed values. Despite these discrepancies, the combined assimilation and reproduction pMoA provided an overall satisfactory description of epoxiconazole effects across the three endpoints. ``` ::: ::: Predicted internal epoxiconazole concentrations increased approximately proportionally with external exposure concentration (@fig-pred_G_EPX_AR_summary_Ciarticle, @tbl-Cirecap). Maximum internal concentrations were generally reached within the first 4-6 days of exposure, considerably earlier than for imidacloprid, and were slightly higher in adults than in juveniles. The estimated no-effect concentration of 47,101 ng$\cdot$g$^{-1}$ was exceeded only at the two highest exposure concentrations, 92.8 and 200 mg$\cdot$kg$^{-1}$. At 20.0 mg$\cdot$kg$^{-1}$ and 43.1 mg$\cdot$kg$^{-1}$, the predicted maximum internal concentration was below the median estimate of the no-effect threshold. However, given the wide credible interval around $c_0$, this exposure condition may still exceed the threshold for part of the posterior distribution.
